summary: Proposes experimental congestion control algorithms for multipath transport such as Multipath TCP. Using several paths at once is more efficient, but single-path algorithms do not suit it, so the paths' congestion control must be coupled. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6356 describes how one multipath connection can share several network paths without taking more than a single TCP flow's share at a shared bottleneck. It coordinates increases in the paths' sending windows, while leaving TCP's response to packet loss unchanged.

subtitle: A congestion controller that coordinates traffic across the paths used by one multipath connection.

tldr.problem: Running ordinary TCP congestion control separately on each subflow can let one multipath connection take more than its fair share at a shared bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: Linked Increases couples the subflows' window increases and limits each subflow to no more aggressive an increase than ordinary TCP would use.
tldr.outcome: It meets the goals of improving throughput and avoiding harm to competing flows, but does not provide full resource pooling. The RFC is Experimental.

today: RFC 6356 is Experimental. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multipath Needs Coordinated Control
sections.content:
Multipath TCP can spread one connection across several paths by creating separate subflows. Each subflow needs its own congestion window, which controls how much data it can send before receiving acknowledgments.

If every subflow runs ordinary TCP congestion control independently, the connection can take more than its fair share when paths cross the same bottleneck. RFC 6356 proposes coupling the subflows' increases to address this problem.
sections.plainLanguage: One connection can send data along several paths at once. If each path speeds up independently, that connection may take too much capacity where the paths meet.

sections.title: Three Goals for a Multipath Controller
sections.content:
The RFC sets three goals: perform at least as well as a single flow on the best available path, avoid taking more from a shared resource than one single-path flow would, and move traffic away from the most congested paths where possible.

The first two goals address throughput and fairness. The third is called resource pooling: using a bundle of paths so that traffic can move away from congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller should match the best single path, avoid taking extra capacity from other users, and shift traffic away from congested paths. The RFC's algorithm fully meets the first two goals, but not the third.

sections.title: How Linked Increases Works
sections.content:
Linked Increases changes only the increase during congestion avoidance. Slow start, fast retransmit, fast recovery and the reduction after a packet drop remain as in standard TCP congestion control.

For each acknowledgment, the increase is the smaller of a coupled increase based on all subflows and the increase ordinary TCP would give that subflow. The parameter alpha sets the overall aggressiveness and is calculated from observed congestion windows and round-trip times.
sections.plainLanguage: When a path gets an acknowledgment, its sending window grows by a coordinated amount. The increase cannot exceed what ordinary TCP would allow on that path.

sections.title: Implementation and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The alpha calculation uses fractional values, so the RFC describes an approximation using integer arithmetic and an alpha_scale parameter. It reports that alpha_scale of 512 works well across a wide range of scenarios, while larger values increase precision and the risk of overflow.

Coupling only increases avoids the insufficient probing and unstable path switching that the RFC associates with fully coupled increase-and-decrease controllers. The result does not move all traffic off higher-loss paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations can approximate the calculation with whole-number arithmetic. Coupling increases lets the sender continue testing paths, but it does not move every bit of traffic to the path with the lowest loss.

sections.title: Traffic-Shifting Attack
sections.content:
An on-path attacker can drop packets on one subflow. The sender then treats that path as congested and shifts more traffic to its other subflows.

The RFC says the effect is limited because the controller makes each path no more aggressive than a single TCP flow. However, a different path may then observe traffic that previously used another path. The RFC says end-to-end encryption is needed when privacy is required.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who can drop packets on one path can cause the sender to use another path more. This controller limits the sending rate, but it does not hide data; use end-to-end encryption for privacy.
